details: RBMK-1000 primary coolant system: forced circulation light water; two main circulation loops (MCL); each loop: 4 main circulation pumps (MCP) of which 3 operating + 1 standby; MCL flow rate: 7000-8000 kg/s per loop (total ~14,000-16,000 kg/s); inlet temperature: 265-270°C; outlet quality: ~14% steam (two-phase boiling flow); outlet pressure: 7.0-7.5 MPa; steam-water separator (SWS) drum: separates steam for turbine from recirculating water; steam flow to turbine: ~5600 kg/s (design); operating point: subcooled water enters fuel channels → bulk boiling along channel length → steam-water mixture exits → SWS drums; 1661 individual fuel channels with separate flow paths
accident_relevance: Importance of two-loop design: during April 26 test: test was measuring coastdown of 1 MCP turbine; turbine trip test → 1 pump coastdown; only 8 MCPs running at reduced power (from 200 MWth vs design 3200 MWth); reduced coolant flow rate at low power → LESS cooling of already-reduced-power core; but ORM=8 = insufficient control rods → power excursion occurred before reduced cooling became limiting; maximum coolant temperature in channels at 200 MWth = well below saturation at 7.5 MPa (saturation T = 290°C); actual failure mode was reactivity not thermal hydraulics at the precursor stage
source: Glasstone Sesonske 1967; INSAG-7 IAEA 1992; rbmk_void_coefficient_physics_REAL.csv; chernobyl_accident_chronology_REAL.csv

details: Critical Heat Flux (CHF) / Departure from Nucleate Boiling (DNB): in RBMK fuel channel under normal operation: heat flux q″ = 200-500 kW/m² (linear power ~14-17 kW/m fuel rod); CHF for vertical annular boiling flow in RBMK pressure tube: ~1500-2000 kW/m² (design safety margin = 3-4×); DNB = transition from nucleate boiling (efficient; low wall temperature) to film boiling (inefficient; wall temperature spikes); in RBMK excursion April 26: power rose from 200 MWth to >30,000 MWth in 4 seconds; heat flux increased 150× instantaneously; CHF exceeded within first second → film boiling → zircaloy cladding temperature 1400→2600°C in seconds; Zr oxidation exothermic reaction (Zr + 2H₂O → ZrO₂ + 2H₂) contributed additional energy
accident_relevance: CHF exceedance sequence: power excursion → CHF exceeded in ms → film boiling → Zr clad overheated → Zr-water reaction → H₂ production → pressure wave → fuel fragmentation → reactivity excursion; first explosion (01:23:44): steam explosion from sudden boiling of bulk coolant in pressure tubes; second explosion (01:23:47): H₂ detonation; Zr-water reaction added ~50 GJ to first explosion energy; each pressure tube ruptured sequentially contributing to progressive fuel dispersal; WHY RBMK is vulnerable: large positive void coefficient + individual pressure tubes (one tube rupture can trigger cascade) + no pressure vessel to contain excursion

details: RBMK vs PWR thermal hydraulic comparison: RBMK: coolant H₂O is moderator + coolant combined; void coefficient positive (+4 to +8 pcm/%void); steam void formation increases reactivity → runaway possible; PWR: coolant H₂O is moderator + coolant combined; void coefficient NEGATIVE (-20 to -100 pcm/%void); steam void formation reduces reactivity → self-limiting; mechanistic explanation: RBMK: heterogeneous design (graphite moderator separate from H₂O coolant); losing H₂O (void) removes H₂O neutron ABSORBER (H₂O captures neutrons with 0.332 barns per H) but graphite moderator remains; NET effect = less absorption → more neutrons → positive feedback; PWR: homogeneous design (H₂O = both moderator AND coolant); losing H₂O reduces BOTH moderation AND absorption; thermally soft spectrum shifts to harder spectrum → more U-238 capture (Doppler) → negative feedback dominant
accident_relevance: At Chernobyl: 200 MWth operation → low coolant flow → subcooled coolant → when power spike began: void fraction increased sharply (coolant flash-boiled in channels) → positive void coefficient amplified reactivity → catastrophic feedback; safety case FAILURE: RBMK designers knew about positive void coefficient; regarded SCRAM (AZ-5) as adequate protection; never analyzed simultaneous ORM=8 + positive void + xenon pit scenario; INSAG-7 conclusion: both design deficiency (positive void) AND operational error (ORM=8) were root causes; removing either eliminates accident; VVER-1000: negative void coefficient → cannot have this accident mode

details: Flow boiling instability in RBMK channels: two-phase flow instability modes: (1) Density Wave Oscillations (DWO): feedback between void fraction and pressure drop → oscillating mass flow rate; period ~1-10 seconds; can cause localized high void → positive reactivity feedback coupling; (2) Ledinegg instability: negative slope region of pressure drop vs flow characteristic → multiple steady states; (3) flashing instability in low-pressure regions; RBMK 1661 parallel channels: individual channel instability can propagate through shared plenum pressure; thermal-hydraulic instability code: DYNAMIC (Soviet); RELAP5 (Western); stability criterion: decay ratio < 1 for all modes
accident_relevance: RBMK stability margin at 200 MWth power (test condition on April 26): thermal-hydraulic models indicate: low power → low coolant flow → REDUCED stability margin compared to full power (3200 MWth); at full power: large flow rate → stable; at 200 MWth with 8 MCPs: potential DWO conditions; Soviet operators were not trained to recognize thermal-hydraulic instability as coupled to reactor instability; operator awareness of neutron-thermal coupling = minimal in 1986 training materials; post-accident: RBMK stability analysis significantly improved; monitoring of coolant voiding at power became explicit operational parameter

details: Steam-Water Separator (SWS) drum in RBMK: large cylindrical pressure vessel at top of reactor; two SWS drums per reactor (one per circulation loop); function: gravity separation of steam from steam-water mixture exiting fuel channels; steam rises → exits to turbine steam lines; saturated water descends → mixed with feedwater → returns to MCP suction; SWS drum pressure = ~7.0 MPa; water inventory in SWS drum = significant thermal storage (acts as buffer); during loss of feedwater: SWS inventory maintains coolant flow for minutes; during test April 26: turbine trip interrupted normal condensate/feedwater flow; SWS steam pressure maintained briefly by stored inventory; turbine coastdown simultaneously ran test measuring this coastdown period
accident_relevance: RBMK SWS drum vs PWR pressurizer: PWR has pressurizer maintaining single-phase liquid pressure; RBMK has two-phase SWS as pressure reference; different pressure control philosophy; SWS water inventory = several hundred tonnes = significant thermal inertia; after April 26 explosion: SWS drums intact initially (explosion localized to reactor hall + Unit 4 reactor building); steam lines to turbine ruptured → large steam release visible from outside as white cloud; first crew visual evidence of accident = massive steam plume from building; on ground: emergency coolant injection (ECCS) initially SWITCHED OFF by operators per test protocol → contributed to rapid core heat-up"

details: Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS) at Chernobyl Unit 4: ECCS purpose: inject cold water to fuel channels if coolant pipe break detected; signal: low coolant pressure in SWS drum; flow: ~800 L/s cold water injection; CRITICAL DECISION April 25-26 1986: Test engineer Aleksandr Dyatlov ordered ECCS disconnected at 01:05 April 25 to prevent test interruption if ECCS automatically fired; ECCS remained disabled through: first test attempt (aborted April 25 for Kiev power demand); 9-hour hold at 1600 MWth; second power reduction attempt; final test run April 25-26; AZ-5 press 01:23:40; explosion 01:23:44; ECCS not re-enabled until after explosion when it was irrelevant
accident_relevance: ECCS bypass = critical operational error: (1) test procedure allowed it (not prohibited explicitly); (2) designers had not flagged ECCS bypass as safety-critical restriction for this type of test; (3) operators believed test would be so brief that ECCS bypass was acceptable; INSAG-7 conclusion: ECCS bypass was one of 6 operational safety violations; BUT: even with ECCS active, the 4-second power excursion (200 MWth → 30,000 MWth) would have been too fast for ECCS to have prevented core destruction; ECCS designed for LOCA (Loss Of Coolant Accident) pipe break scenario → delivers water over minutes; not designed to suppress prompt critical excursion

details: Zirconium-water reaction thermochemistry: Zr + 2H₂O → ZrO₂ + 2H₂; ΔH = -602 kJ/mol Zr (strongly exothermic); onset temperature: ~900°C (significant rate); catastrophic rate: >1200°C; Zr in RBMK fuel cladding: Zr-1%Nb alloy; each RBMK fuel assembly: ~10 kg Zr; total Unit 4 Zr: 1661 channels × 10 kg = 16,610 kg Zr; if all reacted: energy release = 16,610 kg / 0.0913 kg/mol × 602 kJ/mol = ~109,000 GJ; actual fraction reacted = uncertain (explosion dispersed fuel before complete oxidation); estimated 10-30% reacted = 11,000-33,000 GJ from Zr alone; H₂ produced: 16,610 kg Zr × 2mol H₂/mol Zr = 7,330 kg H₂ maximum; detonation energy (H₂): 7330 kg × 141.8 MJ/kg = ~1000 GJ chemical explosive potential
accident_relevance: Second explosion: attributed to H₂ detonation (though steam explosion more likely for first); Zr-water reaction contributed: (1) additional energy beyond fission excursion; (2) H₂ production → flammable/explosive mixture in reactor vault; (3) ZrO₂ ceramic fragments dispersed in explosion debris (graphite blocks + ZrO₂ + UO₂ fuel particles = the 'core debris' seen on roof of Unit 3 and in reactor building environs); comparison: Fukushima Unit 1-3: Zr-water reaction drove H₂ explosions in reactor buildings (containment breach mode different but same chemistry); Chernobyl Zr-water reaction confirmed by: ZrO₂ in debris; H₂ production evidence; post-mortem fuel analysis

details: Graphite combustion in RBMK: graphite (C) + O₂ → CO₂; ΔH = -394 kJ/mol; onset temperature: ~600-700°C in air (graphite is relatively inert below this); RBMK graphite was nuclear-grade (high purity; low boron equivalent; low gas content); 1700 tonnes graphite in Unit 4 core; graphite fire after explosion (April 26-May 9): ignited by: (1) incandescent fuel particles scattered on roof; (2) direct air access to hot graphite through destroyed roof; (3) Wigner energy release partially (stored crystalline disorder from neutron irradiation); helicopter sand/boron/lead/clay drops: 5100 tonnes total; purpose: suppress fire + add neutron absorber + seal core; graphite fire temperature: 1200-1600°C measured by aerial thermometry
accident_relevance: Graphite fire vs Windscale fire 1957: identical mechanism (graphite moderator combustion); Windscale: Wigner energy release in pile 1 graphite as dominant ignition; Chernobyl: prompt criticality excursion + direct air contact dominant; both graphite fires = no containment building → released everything to atmosphere; Chernobyl fire harder to extinguish (1700t vs Windscale ~400t); helicopter drops initially ineffective (sand/boron fell into reactor and were ejected by updraft); fire eventually self-extinguished May 9 as core cooled below ignition temperature; graphite fire = single most important reason for prolonged release (phases 4-6 in source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv)
